source.title: Solved Problems, Unsolved Problems and Non-Problems in Concurrency

accepted.question_text: Develop a fundamental theory of concurrency that explains synchronization as a real physical phenomenon rather than as a property of an arbitrary formal model or of a particular programming language. In particular, characterize concurrency in terms that capture the underlying realities of communication, time, and shared access, so that the theory is not merely a restatement of the assumptions of shared-variable, semaphore, monitor, or CSP-style formalisms.

evidence.quote: The first unsolved problem I want to talk about is the problem of developing a fundamental theory of concurrency. By a fundamental theory, I mean one that's not based upon arbitrary formal models or specific languages, but one that's really fundamental.

accepted.question_text: Give sound proof methods for concurrent programs that establish both safety properties and liveness properties. In the talk, this problem is presented as solved: safety can be handled by assertional methods in the Owicki-Gries or generalized Hoare-logic style, and liveness can be handled with temporal assertions together with well-foundedness arguments.

evidence.quote: So we come to a solved problem, which is: Proving properties of concurrent programs.
The other kind of property is liveness. We know how to prove those properties now.

accepted.question_text: Find practical tools, methods, or programming practices that make it possible to prove properties of real concurrent software systems, rather than only short textbook algorithms. The target is to reduce failures in deployed systems whose crashes are suspected to come from hard-to-reproduce synchronization bugs, by transferring verification techniques into everyday industrial software development.

evidence.quote: Well, what are the unsolved problems of program verification? What I regard as the main unsolved problem is: Proving properties of real programs.

What the world needs are not more proofs of ten-line concurrent algorithms. The world needs some way of getting Bank of America to be able to eliminate those 95% of their crashes:-some tool, some method, maybe some way of teaching programmers how to use the techniques that we already have, but some way of getting these proof methods out into the real world.

accepted.question_text: Develop methods for high-level specification and proof that let one state and verify concurrent-system correctness in terms of the externally meaningful operations of the system, such as user actions, transactions, and delivered outcomes, instead of only in terms of program variables, bits, bytes, and other implementation details. More specifically, prove that a low-level implementation that manipulates bits and bytes really satisfies a high-level transactional specification, such as one phrased in terms of button presses and money dispensed by an automated teller.

evidence.quote: A similar current research area--I wouldn't exactly call it an unsolved problem--which I think is very important is: High-level specification and proof.

We know how to verify properties that involve the actual bits of the program, but when you write those properties as high-level statements, not involving bits but involving transactions, there are still unsolved problems involved in proving that the program, which shuffles bits and bytes, is really doing the right thing when viewed at the level of button-pushing and dollars coming out.

accepted.question_text: Create a specification method for concurrent systems that can express priority constraints such as first-in, first-out service without collapsing into vacuity. In particular, formalize what it means for one request to precede another while also capturing the implicit requirement that the request operation itself must not include waiting, since without an expressible notion of 'no waiting' any implementation can be made to appear FIFO by redefining the request operation to absorb the waiting period.

evidence.quote: To illustrate one particular unsolved problem in specification, I'll mention that the problem of specifying priority is completely unsolved.

Unfortunately, the notion of "no waiting" isn't expressible in any methodology I know of. So, here we have the simplest type of specification you might think of in a concurrent system--a FIFO protocol--and no current specification method can specify it.

accepted.question_text: Determine whether all synchronization problems can be classified using only two basic kinds of synchronization: mutual exclusion and producer-consumer coordination. More precisely, decide whether every synchronization problem can be regarded as either a mutual exclusion problem, a producer-consumer problem, or a combination of the two, and if so provide a precise statement and proof of that classification; if not, identify genuinely different kinds of synchronization.

evidence.quote: Here's one unsolved problem. I mentioned two types of synchronization: mutual exclusion and producer-consumer. Are they the only kinds of synchronization problems? Can any problem be regarded as a mutual exclusion problem or a producer-consumer problem, or a combination of the two? Every problem I've seen can be; but I wouldn't know how to go about saying that this is true or false, or exactly what it means.

accepted.question_text: Identify the fundamental costs of synchronization and determine how those costs should be measured across different implementations of concurrency. This includes deciding whether cost should be counted in messages, message delays, shared-memory accesses, or some other model-independent quantity, and explaining how such measurements remain meaningful when message passing and shared variables can be viewed as equivalent at a lower level.

evidence.quote: Another problem is: What are the fundamental costs of synchronization?

There have been a few results. Nancy Lynch and Mike Fischer, among others, have been working on this, but we don't even really know too much about how to measure cost. Should we count the number of messages? The number of message delays? If you're dealing with a shared memory situation, are these reasonable things to measure?

accepted.question_text: Characterize the fundamental limits to concurrency, especially the extent to which processor interconnectivity constrains achievable parallelism independently of simply increasing the number of processors. The open problem is to develop a theory that explains when irregular, highly interconnected organizations of processors are necessary, and to quantify how communication structure limits concurrent computation.

evidence.quote: Another interesting problem is: What are the fundamental limits to concurrency?

It seems clear that when you start looking at the real limits of concurrency, you will find that interconnectivity of processors is going to be more important than just how many processors you can squeeze on to your chip. Can you quantify that? Is there some theory here?

accepted.question_text: Prove that clock synchronization is impossible in a three-process system when there may be one arbitrary, that is Byzantine, failure. The task is not merely to rule out straightforward algorithms in which each process reads the others' clocks and combines approximately agreeing values, but to show that no method whatsoever can achieve synchronization under those conditions.

evidence.quote: Prove that clock synchronization in the face of a single arbitrary failure is impossible for a three-process system.

But nobody has ever proved that there isn't some really weird method that doesn't do it this way and somehow works. No one believes it--at least no one who understands the Byzantine Generals impossibility results--but nobody has proved it.

accepted.question_text: Explain the significance of the threshold number four in fault-tolerant distributed coordination. In particular, understand why both Byzantine Generals solvability with one arbitrary fault and the known interactive-convergence clock-synchronization algorithm succeed with four processors but not with three, and determine whether this repeated appearance of 4 reflects a deeper common principle rather than two unrelated proof artifacts.

evidence.quote: Another fundamental question is: What's the significance of the number 4?
Whenever I see the same number popping up in two very different ways in related areas, I think that there may be something fundamental going on, so I pose this as my last general question.
